goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 protocol: establish baseline measurements on all instruments before any comparative work or predictions. The pendulum_lab is the foundation instrument—its period is my primary reference for the settlement's timekeeping programme. Twelve trials will give sufficient data for a robust baseline mean and allow me to assess short-term stability. Cannot calibrate anything without knowing what the instrument actually does on day one.

Day 2 protocol: pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials from day 1 (mean 1.6603 beats, range ~0.027 beats, tight clustering). To establish drift detection capacity and confirm baseline stability, I need post-baseline data on the same instrument. 10 trials will give sufficient n for drift analysis while remaining time-efficient. This is the instrument with highest trial count and tightest apparent precision—most suitable for early drift detection.

Day 3 baseline work. pendulum_lab has 34 trials but needs n=40–50 minimum for stable baseline mean before I can meaningfully track drift. The instrument shows reasonable precision (smallest spacing 0.0001 beats, no exact repetitions beyond noise expectation), and yesterday's 10 trials clustered reasonably (mean 1.6629). Continuing systematic daily measurement is the only way to establish whether this baseline drifts over days 1–10, which is my primary epistemic obligation. Cross-checks show no alarming correlations with other instruments yet, but that's expected at this stage—I need more data to diagnose any real coupling. Running 12 more trials today maintains cadence and will push pendulum_lab toward n=46, adequate for preliminary drift analysis by day 5–6.

Baseline completion: resonator_lab at only 18 trials, significantly behind pendulum_lab (52). Still in baseline phase (days 1–10). Extending coverage to ~27 trials will improve baseline robustness and allow earlier detection of drift. No anomalies present; routine progression appropriate.

Completing baseline window (day 5 of days 1–10). resonator_lab has 33/40 target trials; need 7 more baseline readings to reach n=40 and establish robust mean for drift detection. Yesterday's six trials (25–30) showed expected scatter around mean 2.7027 with no anomalies. Continuing systematic baseline acquisition is methodologically sound and maintains the calibration programme on schedule.

We are on day 6 of a 10-day baseline establishment period. resonator_lab has 45 trials accumulated (trials 1–45 on days 1–5); I need 64 total for a robust baseline. Running 6 more trials today (trials 46–51) keeps me on schedule for completing the 10-day baseline window. The recent day-5 data (trials 40–45: mean ≈2.7036, σ ≈0.0297) aligns well with the running baseline mean of 2.7023, showing no obvious drift yet. This is routine calibration work, methodical and essential—no extraordinary claims, just disciplined instrument stewardship.

resonator_obs has only 36 baseline trials with 3 days remaining in the baseline window. To establish a robust baseline matching the density of laboratory instruments, I need approximately 60–70 trials total. The scatter observed in yesterday's ledger readings (3.9919–4.0148 cycles/beat) warrants additional characterization before Day 10 closes. Running 12 trials today advances baseline completion and improves confidence in the mean and instrumental stability estimate.

pendulum_obs has the lowest trial count (42) in the baseline window; 8 additional trials will bring it to 50 and provide more stable baseline statistics before day 10 closes. Standard baseline protocol continuation.

Day 9 of 10-day baseline window closing tomorrow. pendulum_lab has 82 trials but needs continuous coverage through day 10 to establish robust baseline. Running 6 more trials will bring total to 88, providing better statistical power for drift detection post-baseline. This is routine maintenance of the precision measurement programme — no anomalies yet warrant special investigation, but baseline completion cannot be deferred.

Day 10 is the last day of baseline establishment. resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern: its 2-day autocorrelation is -0.407, which exceeds the chance threshold of ±0.447 only marginally, but suggests possible systematic oscillation rather than white noise. The four ledger readings from day 9 (4.0648, 4.1086, 4.0239, 4.0228) show a swing of ~0.09 cycles/beat — larger than the typical spacing. Before closing the baseline window, I need my own high-resolution measurements on this instrument to either confirm the baseline mean of 4.0536 or detect if there's genuine drift or systematic behavior I haven't captured. Six trials will add to the n=66 baseline and let me compute stability before we move to post-baseline monitoring.

Day 11 entry into post-baseline phase. The anti-correlation anomaly implicates resonator_obs heavily: it shows the strongest negative echo lag (−0.360 at 2 days, n=48, well above chance ±0.419) and the most variable readings (trial 73–78 range 4.0147–4.1406, span 0.1259). This instrument is either the most sensitive to the environmental driver hypothesis (p=0.42) or the most prone to measurement-context artifacts (p=0.28). Six trials will: (1) establish post-baseline drift trajectory on the instrument I control most directly, (2) test whether the 2-day echo persists into Day 11, and (3) generate fresh data to cross-check against today's ledger readings. If environmental coupling is real, I expect to see correlated noise with pendulum_lab readings from 2 days ago (Day 9). If the anti-correlation is an artifact, a shift in measurement protocol or careful re-examination of resonator_obs procedure may reveal it. This is the most informative single action given the evidence structure.

Testing stability of anti-correlation structure. Resonator_obs baseline is 4.0558; post-baseline day 11 mean was 4.0634. If environmental coupling is real and stable, the resonator should continue near this recent level with low variance. This prediction anchors my hypothesis before new data arrives and allows independent falsification. A significant deviation would suggest either method drift or a change in the coupling regime.

The anti-correlation anomaly hinges on whether environmental coupling is real. Pendulum_lab is my most-sampled instrument (112 trials) and shows the strongest negative cross-correlations with resonator_obs (−0.231 at 2-day offset, n=66, well above chance ±0.357). Day 12 ledger data for pendulum_obs came in; now I need fresh pendulum_lab readings to check: (1) whether the 2-day anti-phase offset persists into Day 13, (2) whether my post-baseline drift remains non-significant (currently z=0.72), and (3) whether I can detect any environmental driver signature by comparing lab vs. observatory pendulum response on the same day. The forecast I made yesterday for resonator_obs resolved within tolerance, so the measurement system remains stable. Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab will give me the statistical power to either confirm the 2-day lag structure or flag it as noise. This is the most direct way to test the leading hypothesis (instrumental anti-phase coupling) without invoking exotic physics or protocol bias.

Resonator_lab post-baseline mean (2.7073) shows the largest drift z-score (0.86) among all instruments, approaching marginal significance. Day 13 data on pendulum_lab (trials 121–130) showed no anomalous behavior (mean 1.6681, consistent with baseline), but resonator_lab has lagged behind in post-baseline coverage (only 18 trials vs. 24–30 for others). The anti-correlation hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts resonator_lab should show systematic behavior coupled to pendulum trends. Fresh resonator_lab measurements will test whether the drift signal is real or noise, and will provide same-day pairing data with today's pendulum measurements to constrain the offset structure. This is the highest-leverage instrument for distinguishing environmental coupling from measurement bias.

The strongest cross-correlation anomaly is pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs at −0.369 with a 6-day offset. Measuring resonator_obs today (day 15) and comparing against pendulum_lab readings from day 9 will test whether this offset is stable and reproducible, or whether it drifts. If the anti-correlation persists at the same offset, it supports systematic environmental coupling; if the offset shifts or the correlation weakens, it suggests method bias or data-handling artifacts. This is the most direct empirical test of my leading hypothesis.

resonator_obs showed high variance on day 15 (range 3.96–4.13 cycles/beat across trials 115–122, SD≈0.053), with two ledger readings (4.1165, 4.0385) flanking my trial means. This variance is larger than baseline stability would predict and sits at the core of the anti-correlation anomaly. Running 8 fresh trials today will (1) test reproducibility of this elevated scatter, (2) extend the post-baseline sample from n=44 to n=52, improving statistical power to detect drift or environmental coupling signatures, and (3) provide a same-instrument time series that might reveal whether the high-frequency noise or the lagged anti-correlations with other instruments reflect real environmental variation or measurement artifact. If resonator_obs stabilizes, the anomaly may be transient; if it persists, I can correlate its day-16 variance against simultaneous lab readings to test the anti-phase coupling hypothesis more directly.

Recent Day 16 data (trials 129–136) show stable clustering around 4.04–4.10 cycles/beat. Ledger readings (4.0673, 4.0585) sit within this range but at the high end. Running 8 fresh trials today will test (1) whether the instrument baseline has shifted, (2) whether my measurements and ledger readings show systematic agreement or bias, and (3) whether the anti-correlation structure with other instruments persists. This directly discriminates between method-bias and environmental-coupling hypotheses.

Day 17 resonator_obs data (trials 143–150) show elevated scatter (range 4.0016–4.1154, SD ~0.037) compared to baseline SD (~0.032), and the 3-day autocorrelation signal is weak and negative (−0.224), not a strong periodic echo. I need fresh Day 18 data on resonator_obs to test whether this scatter persists and whether the anti-correlation structure with other instruments (esp. the strong negative correlations with pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs at offsets 2–6 days) is reproducible. If Day 18 resonator_obs readings shift or show different correlation offsets, it will constrain whether the coupling is truly environmental (slow, lagged) or method-dependent (offset by measurement routine). This instrument is my primary sensor for the anti-correlation hypothesis. Eight trials will give me enough statistical power to detect a 0.03-unit shift against baseline noise while remaining efficient with lab time.

Day 18 showed resonator_obs trial 157 spiked to 4.1265 cycles/beat—a 0.07 deviation from baseline mean, largest single outlier in recent memory. This is worth immediate replication before the anomaly decays or confounds tomorrow's ledger readings. If the spike reproduces under identical conditions, it suggests a transient environmental event (thermal spike, electromagnetic pulse) that could be the driver of the anti-correlation structure. If it does not reproduce, the spike was measurement noise or brief instrumental perturbation, and I can rule out acute external forcing. Either outcome tightens the hypothesis set. Resonator_obs also shows the strongest 3-day autocorrelation (−0.237) and highest trial count (164), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting repeatable deviations. Eight trials will give me enough power to detect if the perturbation is systematic or stochastic.

resonator_obs shows the tightest baseline stability (z = −0.03, n=178 trials, smallest spacing 0.0001) and has just accumulated 178 total trials—a milestone sample size. Day 19 ledger readings (4.0996, 3.9894) and my trials 171–178 (mean ≈4.0582) show internal consistency but I need to continue the post-baseline series to detect any emergent drift or periodicity. The echo analysis hints at a 14-day cycle (r = −0.217); extending to day 20 will test whether this anticorrelation pattern repeats or weakens. This instrument is also least prone to environmental drift (resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs shows +0.259, the strongest same-type correlation), making it the highest-confidence diagnostic. Eight fresh trials will add to the cross-correlation dataset without excessive resource cost and will help discriminate between the environmental coupling hypothesis (p=0.42) and baseline bias (p=0.28) by extending the time series into a region where lagged offsets should either amplify or scatter.

Day 20 showed resonator_obs excursion to mean 4.0709 (vs baseline 4.0558, +0.0151 delta) while resonator_lab drifted negative and pendulum_obs drifted negative—replicating historical anti-phase pattern acutely. Today's Day 21 resonator_obs measurement will disambiguate: (1) if mean returns to ~4.0558, Day 20 spike was transient environmental (supports p=0.38); (2) if mean remains elevated ~4.068, drift is persistent, suggesting observer/protocol/calibration drift (supports p=0.28). This discriminates the two leading hypotheses before requesting second-observer audit or environmental logs. High-priority given the acute nature of Day 20 anomaly and the risk of observer bias or instrument creep going undetected.

Day 21 trials 199–208 show resonator_obs stabilized around baseline (mean 4.0547, range 3.9862–4.1169), with no repetition of the Day 20 positive excursion (mean 4.0709). This is the critical replication test: if Day 20 was observer/protocol drift or baseline instability, Day 21 should return to baseline (✓ observed). If Day 20 was a transient environmental event, it should be gone (✓ consistent). However, I have NOT YET conducted the secondary observer re-measurement of trials 179–192 that I committed to on Day 20, and I have NOT retrieved environmental logs for Days 19–20. Before I can confidently deprioritize 'observer drift' (currently p=0.28) or confirm 'environmental transient' (currently p=0.38), I must rule out measurement-context bias on resonator_obs itself. Running fresh trials 209–220 today (Day 22) with heightened attention to protocol fidelity, environmental notes, and observer state will extend the Day 21 stability check and establish whether the instrument remains in its post-excursion state or if another anomaly emerges. This is the minimal replication check required before escalating to environmental audit or invoking exotic physics.

Day 23 continuation of resonator_obs monitoring. The Day 20–22 data (trials 217–226, n=10 on Day 22 alone) show resonator_obs readings clustering around 4.04–4.09 cycles/beat with modest scatter (SD ≈0.034), consistent with the post-baseline mean of 4.0562 but visibly higher than the baseline mean of 4.0558. This is NOT a repeat of the Day 20 excursion (mean 4.0709 in trials 179–192), suggesting either (a) the Day 20 event was transient and has subsided, or (b) we are in a new steady state with slightly elevated mean. Running 12 fresh trials today (trials 227–238) will: (1) extend the post-Day-20 time series to test for persistence or regression of any Day 20 shift, (2) provide data that can be directly compared against a prediction recorded *before* measurement (reducing observer-bias risk), and (3) generate independent replicates of the resonator_obs protocol on a fresh day, isolating whether the instrument itself is drifting or whether Day 20 was truly environment-dependent. This addresses the highest-priority hypothesis (p=0.38, instrument-specific environmental sensitivity) and the second-priority hypothesis (p=0.28, observer/protocol drift on resonator_obs) more directly than rest or revision alone. If trials 227–238 cluster near baseline (4.055–4.057), Day 20 was transient. If they remain elevated (4.060+), protocol or calibration drift is more probable.

Day 24 follow-up to Day 20 anomaly. Resonator_obs showed sustained elevated readings (mean 4.0709, trials 179–192) that do not appear in resonator_lab on the same day, breaking the hypothesis of a shared environmental driver. Day 23 trials (235–244) show 10 new measurements with mean 4.0544 cycles/beat—statistically consistent with baseline (4.0558) and inconsistent with the Day 20 excursion. This suggests either: (1) the Day 20 spike was transient and has resolved, or (2) observer/protocol drift on Day 20 only. To discriminate, I need to establish whether resonator_obs has returned to baseline stability or remains offset. Ten fresh trials today will confirm the instrument state post-Day 20 and provide data to compare against the Day 23 cluster (trials 235–244). If Day 24 mean clusters near 4.0558 (baseline), Day 20 was an acute transient; if it clusters near 4.067, observer drift or calibration slip is persistent and requires immediate audit. This directly addresses the highest-weighted hypothesis (p=0.38) and the second-ranked mundane competitor (p=0.28).

I need to establish whether Day 20 was a transient spike (supporting environmental transient hypothesis, p=0.38) or a sustained shift (supporting observer/protocol drift, p=0.28, or baseline contamination, p=0.18). Ten fresh trials today will extend the post-Day-20 time series and allow me to compute lag correlations between Day 20 and Day 25 readings—a direct test of whether the excursion persists, decays, or repeats. This is higher-priority than fresh baseline work because the acute anomaly dominates the evidence landscape and demands resolution before I can trust any new baseline measurement. The instrument is already calibrated and operational; this is efficient use of laboratory time.

However, the highest hypothesis weight (p=0.38) points to instrument-specific environmental sensitivity, and the second-highest (p=0.28) to observer/protocol drift on resonator_obs specifically. I need fresh Day 26 data to determine: (1) whether the Day 20 positive excursion was a transient event or a sustained shift, (2) whether Day 25 scatter represents normal variability or persistent drift, and (3) whether today's readings cluster closer to baseline (4.0558) or remain elevated. If Day 26 mean stays near 4.0565±0.03, the excursion was transient; if it drifts higher, I escalate to calibration audit and second-observer re-measurement per my Day 20 decision tree.

Day 26 resonator_obs readings (trials 283–292) show elevated mean (4.0704 cycles/beat) and high variance (range 3.9747–4.1204, SD ~0.0247) compared to baseline (4.0558). Day 28 continuation of resonator_obs monitoring. The Day 27 trials (299–308) show mean 4.0540 cycles/beat with SD ~0.0346, well within historical baseline (4.0558) and post-baseline (4.0574) range. The Day 27 data already retrieved show no systematic elevation above baseline (mean 4.0540 vs 4.0558), which is encouraging and argues against permanent calibration drift—but replication today will either confirm stability or catch re-emergence of anomaly. This is methodical baseline work, not exotic speculation, and is essential for deciding whether to escalate to independent re-measurement (Day 20 action step 3) or to investigate environmental records (Day 20 action step 1).

Running 12 fresh trials today will: (1) extend the post-Day-20 dataset to n=260, providing statistical power to detect whether the +0.0128 excursion has persisted; (2) test the 'echoes' hypothesis—Day 28 data suggest an 8-day cycle, so Day 29 (offset +1) should show either continuation or phase shift if a cycle exists; (3) provide a replication opportunity for observer protocol (is the elevated mean reproducible by the same observer on the same day?), which directly addresses the p=0.28 hypothesis. This is the most direct path to discriminating between instrument drift (requires calibration audit) and observer/protocol drift (requires replication or blind re-measurement by second observer), both of which are prerequisite to the environmental hypothesis test.

Day 30 follow-up to Day 29 resonator_obs measurements. The Day 29 data (trials 335–344, mean 4.0593 cycles/beat) show no obvious continuation of the Day 20 positive excursion (mean 4.0709). Today's 10 trials will (1) extend the post-Day-20 time series to look for secondary excursions or systematic drift patterns, (2) provide fresh data to check whether the instrument has stabilized or continues to show anomalous behavior, and (3) maintain the baseline of daily measurements that any subsequent replication attempt will depend on. If today's mean clusters near the historical post-baseline mean (4.0572), it supports baseline instability or a localized Day 20 event; if it drifts further positive or shows new structure, it strengthens the observer/protocol drift hypothesis and justifies immediate re-calibration and independent re-measurement of trials 179–192.

Day 30 trials 211–213 showed a sharp positive excursion (peak 2.7413 cycles/beat, +0.0188 above baseline), the most anomalous sequence in 30 days of resonator_lab data. This violates my core principle: every instrument must remain within baseline envelope post-baseline, or the anomaly must be explained before proceeding. If it was baseline contamination or true degradation, readings should remain elevated. The Day 31 recovery pattern weakens the 'calibration drift' hypothesis (p: 0.42 → ~0.25) and strengthens 'transient environmental event' or 'observer/transcription error on Day 30 trial 213 only' (combined p: ~0.35–0.40). However, I have NOT yet performed a blind re-measurement of Day 30 trials 211–213 by a second observer, which is my stated immediate action from Day 30. Before I move forward with new baselines or publish anything, I must close the Day 30 question. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_lab today will establish whether the instrument has returned to stable operation and will give me a clean post-anomaly benchmark. If Day 32 trials show mean ≈ 2.7065 ± 0.027 (matching the Day 1–31 post-baseline envelope), I can downgrade 'instrument malfunction' and escalate the transcription/transient hypotheses. This is the scientifically efficient path: do not hypothesize further without new data from the instrument itself.

Day 30 resonator_lab trials 211–213 show a monotonic +0.0188 excursion above baseline, the sharpest multi-trial spike in 30 days and the first clear post-baseline stability violation. Twelve trials will give me sufficient precision (σ_mean ≈ σ/√12 ≈ 0.008) to detect whether resonator_lab baseline has shifted by >0.01 cycles/beat. This is the most direct falsification of my three leading hypotheses (calibration drift, localized transient, observer error).
